newsitem.title: UK: Sinn Fein suggests new IRA truce in sight.
newsitem.headline: Sinn Fein suggests new IRA truce in sight.

text.p: A senior official of the IRA's political wing said on Saturday that the Irish guerrillas might renew the truce they called off nine months ago.

Martin McGuinness, Sinn Fein's chief negotiator, held out the prospect of an Irish Republican Army ceasefire if British Prime Minister John Major accepted a formula tabled by peace broker John Hume, leader of the moderate nationalist SDLP.
Britain's supporters in Northern Ireland warned London not to do deals with the republicans and a British spokesman said any new ceasefire must be "absolutely unequivocal."
McGuinness said Sinn Fein, which wants a guaranteed place in unconditional all-party talks, would try to get the IRA to reinstate a truce abandoned in February if Britain agreed to Hume's proposals.
Hume has declined to specify his suggestions but says they are geared towards providing "reassurance" about the nature of all-party talks and the comprehensive nature of a talks agenda.
Speaking before the opening on Saturday of a special Sinn Fein conference called to review its "peace strategy", McGuinness told BBC radio.
"If we can achieve all that we have identified, which we believe is very reasonable indeed, then we are prepared to do that again," he told BBC radio.

"I think there would be considerable hope that we could manage to succeed a second time around. But it will be much more difficult, of course, because of the very great distrust which exists between the British government and the IRA," he added.
His comments drew an angry response from hardline pro-British Protestant politician Peter Robinson, who suggested Britain might weaken its position to accept a new IRA ceasefire.

"I have no doubt that if the prime minister were to cave into the IRA's demands, they would call a ceasefire. But...(that) would be unacceptable to the Unionist community in Northern Ireland," Robinson told Reuters.
"It seems that people are going through what has already been prepared to be another tactical cessation of violence for the IRA," said Robinson, deputy leader of the Democratic Unionist Partry.

Reg Empey, vice president of the powerful Ulster Unionist Party, said Major should end speculation by letting the public know what he had been discussing with Hume, who has had talks with Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams.

The IRA, the main guerrilla force fighting British rule in Northern Ireland, declared a truce in September 1994. But it broke the ceasefire in February and has launched bomb attacks in England and at military bases in Germany and Northern Ireland.
The one-day Sinn Fein conference is being held behind closed doors in the village of Athboy in Ireland.
Sinn Fein sources said the conference would discuss "conflict resolution processes".

The Irish Times newspaper reported that the conference would hear details of a special meeting of IRA commanders three weeks ago which reportedly endorsed the party's attempts to win a seat in all-party talks.

On Thursday a republican splinter group, the Irish Continuity Army Council, claimed responsibilty for planting a huge bomb that was defused outside police headquarters in the Northern Irish city of Londonderry.
